text: A privacy impact assessment, GDPR's version is called a DPIA, is a structured review of a planned data processing activity, done before it launches, to find privacy risks and decide how to address them before the system ever touches personal data.

GDPR Article 35 requires a DPIA specifically when processing is likely to result in high risk, large-scale processing of sensitive data and systematic monitoring are the examples the regulation calls out. A usable PIA, whatever template it uses, answers five questions. What data and why, exactly what's involved and the specific purpose. Is it necessary and proportionate, could the same purpose be achieved with less data. What are the risks to individuals, not just could we get breached, but what actually happens to a real person. What mitigates those risks, tying directly back to classification, access restriction, masking, and retention limits. And who signed off, a named reviewer confirming the assessment was actually done.

Running Brightfield's dashboard project through a PIA, the what data and why question alone would have forced someone to notice the project only needed aggregated regional totals, not row-level customer records with payment fragments. The necessity question would have flagged the broad access grant immediately, a regional sales summary doesn't need read access to individual shipping addresses. A PIA wouldn't replace the access governance model, it would have caught the problem at design time instead of relying entirely on a recertification cycle months later.

This closes Data Security, Privacy and Classification. Sensitive data foundations, classification, access control, data protection techniques, lifecycle and compliance, and applied case studies, thirty lessons building one connected judgment. The Data Governance path continues next with Microsoft Purview, the platform where many of these concepts get implemented hands-on in a real enterprise governance tool.

Classify before you expose, grant the minimum, log what happened, know your obligations before an incident forces you to learn them. Those ideas don't go out of date the way a tool's interface eventually does. Congratulations on finishing the course.
